title: Bronze Health Insurance Plan
content:
Bronze plans have the lowest monthly premiums of all plan categories in the Health Insurance Marketplace. Bronze plans cover approximately 60% of healthcare costs on average, while the member pays about 40%. These plans are best suited for healthy individuals who don't expect to use many health services but want protection against worst-case medical scenarios like serious illness or injury.

Key features of Bronze plans:
• Lowest monthly premium payments
• Highest deductibles (typically $6,000-$8,000 for individuals)
• Higher copays and coinsurance when you get care
• Cover all essential health benefits including preventive care at no cost
• 3 primary care visits before deductible in some plans
• Good choice for young, healthy adults
• Can be paired with a Health Savings Account (HSA) if the plan is HSA-eligible

Bronze plans cover all 10 essential health benefits required by the Affordable Care Act:
1. Ambulatory patient services (outpatient care)
2. Emergency services
3. Hospitalization
4. Pregnancy, maternity, and newborn care
5. Mental health and substance use disorder services
6. Prescription drugs
7. Rehabilitative and habilitative services
8. Laboratory services
9. Preventive and wellness services
10. Pediatric services including dental and vision

title: Silver Health Insurance Plan
content:
Silver plans offer a moderate balance between monthly premium costs and out-of-pocket costs when you get care. Silver plans cover approximately 70% of healthcare costs on average, with the member paying about 30%.

Key features of Silver plans:
• Moderate monthly premiums (higher than Bronze, lower than Gold)
• Moderate deductibles (typically $3,000-$5,000 for individuals)
• Lower copays and coinsurance than Bronze plans
• ONLY plan category eligible for cost-sharing reductions (CSRs)
• If your income is between 100-250% of the federal poverty level, Silver plans offer extra savings
• Cost-sharing reductions lower your deductible, copays, and maximum out-of-pocket costs
• Most popular plan category on the Marketplace

Why Silver plans are special:
Silver is the only plan category where you can get cost-sharing reductions (CSR). If eligible based on income, you get a Silver plan that effectively works like a Gold or Platinum plan at Silver prices. This makes Silver plans the best value for many consumers, especially those with lower incomes.

Cost-sharing reduction tiers:
• 100-150% FPL: Plan covers ~94% of costs (like a Platinum plan)
• 150-200% FPL: Plan covers ~87% of costs (better than Gold)
• 200-250% FPL: Plan covers ~73% of costs (slightly better than standard Silver)

title: Gold Health Insurance Plan
content:
Gold plans have higher monthly premiums but lower costs when you get care. Gold plans cover approximately 80% of healthcare costs on average, with the member paying about 20%.

Key features of Gold plans:
• Higher monthly premiums than Bronze and Silver
• Lower deductibles (typically $1,000-$2,500 for individuals)
• Lower copays when you visit the doctor or fill prescriptions
• Good for people who expect to use a lot of medical services
• Recommended for those managing chronic conditions
• Predictable healthcare costs throughout the year
• Not eligible for cost-sharing reductions

Gold plans are best for:
• Families with children who need regular doctor visits
• Individuals with ongoing medical conditions (diabetes, asthma, heart disease)
• People who take expensive prescription medications regularly
• Anyone who expects surgery or other major medical procedures
• Those who prefer higher premiums for lower surprise costs

title: Platinum Health Insurance Plan
content:
Platinum plans have the highest monthly premiums but the lowest costs when you get care. Platinum plans cover approximately 90% of healthcare costs on average, with the member paying only about 10%.

Key features of Platinum plans:
• Highest monthly premiums of all categories
• Very low deductibles (often $0-$500 for individuals)
• Lowest copays and coinsurance
• Best for people who need a lot of healthcare services
• Most predictable costs — you know what you'll pay each month
• Maximum out-of-pocket costs are the lowest of all plan types
• Not available in all areas of the Marketplace

Platinum plans are best for:
• People with serious or chronic health conditions
• Those who see specialists frequently
• Individuals taking multiple or expensive medications
• People who want the most comprehensive coverage with minimal surprise bills

title: Catastrophic Health Insurance Plan
content:
Catastrophic plans are a low-cost option available to people under 30 or those who qualify for a hardship or affordability exemption. These plans protect you from worst-case scenarios like serious illness or injury.

Key features of Catastrophic plans:
• Very low monthly premiums (lowest available)
• Very high deductible (equal to the annual out-of-pocket maximum)
• Cover 3 primary care visits per year before meeting the deductible
• Cover all essential health benefits after the deductible is met
• Free preventive care services (like all Marketplace plans)
• Cannot use premium tax credits to lower your costs
• Only available to people under 30 or those with exemptions

How catastrophic plans work:
You pay all medical costs up to a high deductible amount. After that, the plan covers all essential health benefits. These plans are designed as a safety net — you get free preventive care and 3 doctor visits per year, but for everything else, you pay full price until you hit the deductible.

Eligibility requirements:
• Under 30 years old on the plan start date, OR
• Have a hardship exemption, OR
• Have an affordability exemption (lowest-priced coverage is more than 8.39% of income)

title: Health Insurance Marketplace Eligibility Rules
content:
To be eligible for health insurance through the Health Insurance Marketplace (also known as the Exchange), you must meet the following requirements:

Basic eligibility requirements:
• Live in the United States
• Be a U.S. citizen or national (or be lawfully present)
• Not be currently incarcerated
• Not be enrolled in Medicare

Open Enrollment Period:
The annual Open Enrollment Period typically runs from November 1 to January 15. During this time, anyone eligible can sign up for or change their health insurance plan.

Special Enrollment Period (SEP):
Outside of Open Enrollment, you can sign up if you experience a qualifying life event:
• Losing existing health coverage (job loss, aging off parent's plan)
• Getting married or divorced
• Having a baby or adopting a child
• Moving to a new area with different plan options
• Changes in household income that affect subsidy eligibility
• Turning 26 and losing coverage under a parent's plan
• Becoming a U.S. citizen
• Leaving incarceration

Income-based assistance:
• Premium Tax Credits: Available if income is between 100-400% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL)
• Cost-Sharing Reductions: Available with Silver plans if income is 100-250% FPL
• Medicaid: May qualify if income is below 138% FPL (in expansion states)
• CHIP: Children may qualify for low-cost coverage through the Children's Health Insurance Program

2024 Federal Poverty Level (FPL) Guidelines (48 contiguous states):
• 1 person: $15,060
• 2 people: $20,440
• 3 people: $25,820
• 4 people: $31,200
• Add $5,380 for each additional person

title: Essential Health Benefits - What Must Be Covered
content:
Under the Affordable Care Act (ACA), all Marketplace health insurance plans must cover 10 categories of essential health benefits. Insurance companies cannot deny coverage or charge more based on pre-existing conditions.

The 10 Essential Health Benefits:

1. Ambulatory Patient Services (Outpatient Care)
   • Doctor visits without being admitted to a hospital
   • Outpatient surgery
   • Specialist visits

2. Emergency Services
   • Emergency room visits
   • Cannot charge more for out-of-network emergency care
   • Stabilization services

3. Hospitalization
   • Inpatient hospital stays
   • Surgery requiring hospital admission
   • Overnight observation

4. Pregnancy, Maternity, and Newborn Care
   • Prenatal visits and screenings
   • Labor and delivery
   • Postnatal care for mother and baby
   • Breastfeeding support and supplies

5. Mental Health and Substance Use Disorder Services
   • Behavioral health treatment
   • Counseling and psychotherapy
   • Substance abuse treatment
   • Must be covered at parity with medical/surgical benefits

6. Prescription Drugs
   • At least one drug in every category and class
   • Coverage for generic and brand-name drugs
   • Plans have formularies listing covered medications

7. Rehabilitative and Habilitative Services and Devices
   • Physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy
   • Services to help recover or develop skills
   • Durable medical equipment

8. Laboratory Services
   • Blood tests, urinalysis, imaging
   • Diagnostic testing
   • Pathology services

9. Preventive and Wellness Services and Chronic Disease Management
   • Annual wellness visits at no cost
   • Immunizations and screenings
   • Chronic disease management programs

10. Pediatric Services Including Dental and Vision
    • Children's dental check-ups
    • Children's eye exams and glasses
    • Developmental screenings

title: Health Insurance Costs Explained - Premiums, Deductibles, Copays
content:
Understanding health insurance costs involves four key components: premiums, deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. Here's how each works:

PREMIUM:
Your monthly payment to have health insurance. You pay this whether or not you use medical services. Think of it like a membership fee.
• Paid monthly to your insurance company
• Lower premiums usually mean higher deductibles
• Premium Tax Credits can lower your monthly premium if you qualify

DEDUCTIBLE:
The amount you pay for covered health care services before your insurance plan starts paying. For example, with a $2,000 deductible, you pay the first $2,000 of covered services yourself.
• Resets each plan year (usually January 1)
• Preventive care is covered before meeting your deductible
• Family plans have both individual and family deductibles
• Typical range: $0 (Platinum) to $8,000+ (Catastrophic)

COPAYMENT (COPAY):
A fixed amount you pay for a covered health care service after you've met your deductible. For example, $25 for a doctor visit or $15 for a prescription.
• Fixed dollar amount per service
• May vary by service type (primary care vs. specialist)
• Some plans offer copays before meeting the deductible

COINSURANCE:
Your share of the costs of a covered health care service, calculated as a percentage. For example, if coinsurance is 20%, you pay 20% and insurance pays 80%.
• Percentage-based cost sharing
• Applies after you've met your deductible
• Varies by plan category (Bronze: ~40%, Silver: ~30%, Gold: ~20%, Platinum: ~10%)

OUT-OF-POCKET MAXIMUM:
The most you have to pay for covered services in a plan year. After you reach this amount, your plan pays 100% of covered services.
• 2024 limit: $9,450 for individuals, $18,900 for families
• Includes deductibles, copays, and coinsurance
• Premiums do NOT count toward the out-of-pocket maximum
• Once reached, plan pays 100% for the rest of the year

title: How to File a Health Insurance Claim
content:
Filing a health insurance claim is the process of requesting payment from your insurance company for medical services you've received. Here's how the claims process works:

When do you need to file a claim?
• Most in-network providers file claims directly with your insurance (no action needed from you)
• You may need to file yourself if you see an out-of-network provider
• You may need to file if a provider doesn't accept your insurance

Steps to file a health insurance claim:

Step 1: Get an itemized bill from your healthcare provider
• Request a detailed bill showing each service, procedure code, and charge
• Make sure it includes the provider's tax ID number

Step 2: Complete a claim form
• Get the form from your insurance company's website or by calling them
• Fill out your policy number, group number, and patient information
• Attach the itemized bill and any supporting documents

Step 3: Submit the claim
• Mail, fax, or submit online through your insurer's member portal
• Keep copies of everything you submit
• Note the submission date for your records

Step 4: Wait for processing
• Insurance companies typically process claims within 30 days
• You'll receive an Explanation of Benefits (EOB) showing what was covered
• The EOB is NOT a bill — it explains how the claim was processed

Step 5: Pay your share
• After processing, you'll receive a bill for any amount you owe
• This may include your deductible, copay, or coinsurance

If your claim is denied:
• Review the denial reason in the EOB
• You have the right to appeal any denied claim
• Internal appeal: Ask your insurance company to reconsider
• External review: An independent third party reviews the decision
• File appeals within the timeframe specified (usually 180 days)

title: Free Preventive Care Services Covered by All Plans
content:
All Marketplace health insurance plans must cover certain preventive services at no cost to you — no copay, no coinsurance, and no deductible. These services are free when provided by an in-network provider.

Preventive services for all adults:
• Blood pressure screening
• Cholesterol screening (for adults at higher risk)
• Colorectal cancer screening (adults 45-75)
• Depression screening
• Diabetes (Type 2) screening (for adults with high blood pressure)
• Diet counseling (for adults at higher risk for chronic disease)
• HIV screening (for everyone ages 15-65 and other ages at increased risk)
• Immunization vaccines (flu, hepatitis A & B, HPV, measles, mumps, rubella, tetanus, varicella)
• Lung cancer screening (annual LDCT for adults 50-80 with smoking history)
• Obesity screening and counseling
• Sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention counseling and screening
• Statin preventive medication (for adults 40-75 at higher risk)
• Tobacco use screening and cessation interventions

Preventive services for women:
• Breast cancer mammography screening (every 1-2 years for women over 40)
• Cervical cancer screening (Pap test)
• Contraception — FDA-approved methods, sterilization, education
• Breastfeeding support, supplies, and counseling
• Osteoporosis screening (women over 60)
• Prenatal care visits and screenings
• Well-woman visits
• Domestic violence screening and counseling

Preventive services for children:
• Autism screening (18 and 24 months)
• Behavioral assessments
• Blood pressure screening
• Developmental screening (under age 3)
• Fluoride supplements and dental screening
• Hearing screening for newborns
• Height, weight, and BMI measurements
• Immunizations (DTaP, Hep A & B, Hib, HPV, MMR, Polio, and more)
• Lead screening
• Vision screening

IMPORTANT: Preventive services are only free when:
• Performed by an in-network provider
• The visit is specifically for prevention (not treatment of symptoms)
• Following recommended frequency guidelines

title: Types of Health Insurance Plans - HMO, PPO, EPO, POS
content:
Health insurance plans use different networks of doctors and hospitals. Understanding network types helps you choose the right plan:

HMO (Health Maintenance Organization):
• Must choose a Primary Care Physician (PCP)
• Need referrals from PCP to see specialists
• Generally only covers in-network care (except emergencies)
• Lower premiums and out-of-pocket costs
• Less flexibility but more coordinated care
• Best for: People who don't mind having a PCP coordinate their care

PPO (Preferred Provider Organization):
• No PCP requirement
• No referrals needed to see specialists
• Can see out-of-network providers (but at higher cost)
• Higher premiums than HMO
• More flexibility in choosing providers
• Best for: People who want flexibility and are willing to pay more

EPO (Exclusive Provider Organization):
• No PCP requirement
• No referrals needed
• Only covers in-network providers (except emergencies)
• Lower premiums than PPO
• Moderate flexibility within the network
• Best for: People who want some flexibility without paying PPO prices

POS (Point of Service):
• Must choose a PCP
• Need referrals for specialists
• Can see out-of-network providers (at higher cost)
• Moderate premiums
• Combines features of HMO and PPO
• Best for: People who want coordinated care but occasional out-of-network access

How to check if your doctor is in-network:
• Use your insurance company's online provider directory
• Call the doctor's office and provide your insurance information
• Call the number on the back of your insurance card
• Check during Open Enrollment before selecting a plan

title: Health Insurance Lead Qualification Criteria
content:
Lead qualification criteria for health insurance sales. Use these rules to determine if a prospect is a qualified lead:

TIER 1 - HIGHLY QUALIFIED LEAD:
Score: 80-100 points
• Age 26-64 (prime health insurance market)
• Currently uninsured or insurance expiring within 60 days
• Household income 150-400% FPL (eligible for subsidies)
• Expressed explicit interest in getting coverage
• Located in a serviceable area
• Can make purchasing decision independently
• Has budget for monthly premiums ($200-$800/month range)

TIER 2 - QUALIFIED LEAD:
Score: 50-79 points
• Age 18-25 or 65+ (specific plan needs)
• Has insurance but wants to switch or compare
• Income may qualify for Medicaid or higher-tier plans
• Interested but needs more information
• Family coverage needed (spouse, dependents)
• Has some pre-existing conditions (not a barrier under ACA)

TIER 3 - NURTURE LEAD:
Score: 20-49 points
• Not currently looking to purchase
• Covered by employer insurance (may change during Open Enrollment)
• Browsing for future reference
• Age under 18 (parent/guardian needed)
• Income uncertain or not disclosed

DISQUALIFIED:
Score: 0-19 points
• Already has Medicare (cannot use Marketplace)
• Not a U.S. citizen or lawfully present
• Currently incarcerated
• Requesting services outside our coverage area
• Not willing to provide any personal information

Qualification questions to ask:
1. "What is your current insurance situation?" (coverage status)
2. "How many people need coverage?" (family size)
3. "What is your approximate household income?" (subsidy eligibility)
4. "Do you have any ongoing medical conditions?" (plan recommendation)
5. "What's most important to you — lower monthly payments or lower costs at the doctor?" (plan fit)
6. "Are you currently seeing any doctors you'd want to keep?" (network needs)
7. "When do you need coverage to start?" (urgency/timeline)

title: Common Health Insurance Objections and Responses
content:
Common objections encountered during health insurance lead qualification and recommended response strategies:

OBJECTION 1: "It's too expensive / I can't afford insurance"
Response: I understand cost is a concern. Many people don't realize they qualify for financial help. Based on your income, you might qualify for premium tax credits that can significantly lower your monthly payment — sometimes to as low as $0-$50 per month. Would you like me to check what subsidies you might be eligible for?

OBJECTION 2: "I'm healthy, I don't need insurance"
Response: That's great that you're healthy! Health insurance isn't just for when you're sick, though. It also covers free preventive care like annual check-ups, screenings, and vaccinations. Plus, accidents and unexpected illnesses can happen to anyone — a single emergency room visit can cost $3,000-$10,000 without insurance. Many young, healthy people choose a Bronze or Catastrophic plan for low monthly costs with protection against major medical bills.

OBJECTION 3: "I need to think about it / talk to my spouse"
Response: Absolutely, this is an important decision. I'd be happy to give you time. Would it help if I sent you a summary of the plans we discussed so you can review them together? I can also schedule a callback at a time that works for both of you. When would be a good time?

OBJECTION 4: "I don't trust insurance companies"
Response: I hear that concern a lot, and it's valid. The good news is that under the Affordable Care Act, insurance companies must follow strict rules — they can't deny you for pre-existing conditions, must cover essential health benefits, and must spend at least 80% of your premiums on actual healthcare. If they don't, they have to give you a rebate. You also have the right to appeal any denied claim.

OBJECTION 5: "The enrollment process is too complicated"
Response: I completely understand — it can seem overwhelming. That's exactly why I'm here to help. I can walk you through the entire process step by step. Most people complete their enrollment in about 15-20 minutes with guidance. Would you like me to help you get started right now?

OBJECTION 6: "I missed the enrollment period"
Response: Open Enrollment runs from November 1 to January 15 each year. However, you may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period if you've experienced a qualifying life event — like losing other coverage, getting married, having a baby, or moving. Have any of these happened to you in the last 60 days?

OBJECTION 7: "My employer offers insurance, why do I need this?"
Response: Employer-sponsored insurance is often a great option! If your employer offers affordable coverage that meets minimum standards, that's typically the best path. However, if your employer's plan costs more than 8.39% of your household income for self-only coverage, or doesn't meet minimum value requirements, you may qualify for Marketplace subsidies instead. Would you like me to help you compare?

OBJECTION 8: "I'll just pay the penalty / go without"
Response: Actually, the individual mandate penalty was reduced to $0 at the federal level starting in 2019, so there's no federal penalty for being uninsured. However, some states like California, Massachusetts, and New Jersey have their own mandates with penalties. More importantly, going without insurance means you're one accident or illness away from potentially devastating medical bills. Emergency room visits alone average $2,000-$3,000.

OBJECTION 9: "I want to compare more plans first"
Response: That's a smart approach! I can actually help you compare plans right now. I have access to all available plans in your area, and I can show you side-by-side comparisons based on your specific needs — premiums, deductibles, covered doctors, and estimated total costs. What factors are most important to you in choosing a plan?

OBJECTION 10: "I had a bad experience with insurance before"
Response: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about what happened? I want to make sure we address those concerns. The healthcare landscape has changed significantly — there are now protections in place for consumers, and many plans have improved their networks and customer service. Let's find a plan that addresses the specific issues you faced before.

title: Frequently Asked Questions About Health Insurance
content:
General frequently asked questions about health insurance:

Q: What is a health insurance premium?
A: A premium is the amount you pay each month to have health insurance coverage. You must pay this regardless of whether you use healthcare services.

Q: What is a deductible?
A: A deductible is the amount you pay for healthcare services before your insurance starts to pay. For example, with a $1,500 deductible, you pay the first $1,500 of covered services yourself.

Q: Can I be denied coverage for pre-existing conditions?
A: No. Under the Affordable Care Act, insurance companies cannot deny you coverage or charge you more because of a pre-existing condition. This applies to all Marketplace plans.

Q: When can I sign up for health insurance?
A: You can sign up during the annual Open Enrollment Period (November 1 - January 15). Outside this period, you may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period if you have a qualifying life event.

Q: What are premium tax credits?
A: Premium tax credits are government subsidies that lower your monthly premium. You may qualify if your household income is between 100-400% of the Federal Poverty Level and you don't have affordable employer coverage.

Q: How do I choose between an HMO and PPO?
A: HMOs typically have lower premiums but require you to use in-network providers and get referrals. PPOs offer more flexibility to see any doctor but cost more. Choose HMO if cost is a priority; choose PPO if flexibility matters more.

Q: What happens if I go to an out-of-network doctor?
A: With HMO/EPO plans, out-of-network care generally isn't covered (except emergencies). With PPO/POS plans, you can see out-of-network doctors but will pay more. Always check your plan's network before scheduling appointments.

Q: Can I keep my doctor if I switch plans?
A: It depends on whether your doctor participates in the new plan's network. Before switching, check the plan's provider directory or call your doctor to confirm they accept the new insurance.

Q: What is the out-of-pocket maximum?
A: The most you'll have to pay for covered services in a year. After reaching this amount, your insurance pays 100% of covered services. For 2024, the maximum is $9,450 for individuals.

Q: What is preventive care and is it really free?
A: Preventive care includes services like annual check-ups, vaccinations, cancer screenings, and wellness visits. All Marketplace plans must cover these at no cost when you use in-network providers.

Q: How do I file a complaint about my insurance company?
A: Contact your state's Department of Insurance or the federal marketplace at 1-800-318-2596. You can also file a complaint with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

Q: What is COBRA and how does it work?
A: COBRA allows you to temporarily continue your employer's health insurance after leaving a job. You must pay the full premium (including the portion your employer used to pay) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA coverage typically lasts 18 months.

title: Health Insurance Glossary of Key Terms
content:
Important health insurance terms and their definitions:

Allowed Amount: The maximum amount a plan will pay for a covered health care service. Also called "eligible expense," "payment allowance," or "negotiated rate."

Appeal: A request for your insurance company or the Marketplace to review a decision that denies a benefit or payment.

Balance Billing: When a provider bills you for the difference between the provider's charge and the allowed amount. In-network providers generally cannot balance bill you.

Beneficiary: A person who is eligible for or receiving benefits under an insurance policy.

Benefit Year: The calendar year in which benefits are provided. Most Marketplace plans run January 1 through December 31.

Claim: A request by you or your provider to your insurance company for payment for services received.

COBRA: Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act — allows temporary continuation of employer health coverage after job loss.

Copayment (Copay): A fixed amount you pay for a covered service, typically at the time of service.

Coinsurance: Your share of costs of a covered service, calculated as a percentage of the allowed amount.

Cost-Sharing Reduction (CSR): A discount that lowers the amount you pay for deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. Available only with Silver plans if your income qualifies.

Deductible: The amount you pay for covered services before your plan begins to pay.

Dependent: A child or other individual who is eligible for coverage under a subscriber's health plan.

EPO (Exclusive Provider Organization): A plan that only covers in-network care, except in emergencies.

Essential Health Benefits (EHB): The 10 categories of services all Marketplace plans must cover.

Explanation of Benefits (EOB): A statement from your insurance company showing what was billed, allowed, and paid for a claim.

Formulary: A list of prescription drugs covered by a health plan.

HMO (Health Maintenance Organization): A plan requiring you to choose a primary care physician and get referrals for specialists.

In-Network: Providers and facilities that have a contract with your insurance plan, resulting in lower costs for you.

Marketplace: The government exchange where you can compare and buy health insurance plans (Healthcare.gov or state-based).

Out-of-Network: Providers without a contract with your plan, resulting in higher costs.

Out-of-Pocket Maximum: The most you pay during a policy period before your plan begins to pay 100%.

POS (Point of Service): A plan combining HMO and PPO features with referral requirements.

PPO (Preferred Provider Organization): A plan offering more flexibility to see any provider without referrals.

Pre-existing Condition: A health condition that existed before coverage begins. Under the ACA, insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more for pre-existing conditions.

Premium: The monthly amount paid for health insurance.

Premium Tax Credit: A government subsidy that reduces monthly premium costs for eligible individuals.

Primary Care Physician (PCP): A doctor who provides general health care and coordinates specialist referrals.

Prior Authorization: A requirement that your provider get approval from your plan before a specific service is covered.

Referral: A recommendation from your PCP to see a specialist, required by some plan types.

Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC): A document that provides consistent, plain-language information about a plan's costs and coverage.

title: Insurance Agent Compliance and Required Disclosures
content:
Required compliance disclosures and regulations for health insurance agents and representatives:

REQUIRED DISCLOSURES:
1. Agent/Broker Identification: Must clearly identify yourself and the company you represent at the beginning of every call.

2. Recording Disclosure: If calls are being recorded, you must inform the customer at the start: "This call may be recorded for quality and training purposes."

3. Not Medical Advice: Must state that information provided is not medical advice. "Please note that I am providing insurance information, not medical advice. Consult your healthcare provider for medical questions."

4. No Guarantee of Coverage: Cannot guarantee specific coverage or benefits without reviewing plan documents. "Specific coverage details are subject to plan terms and conditions."

5. Scope of Appointment: Before discussing specific products, should establish the scope of the conversation and types of plans the customer is interested in.

PROHIBITED PRACTICES:
• Cannot make false or misleading statements about coverage or benefits
• Cannot pressure customers into purchasing decisions
• Cannot discriminate based on health status, age, gender, or disability
• Cannot share customer personal information without consent
• Cannot cold-call Medicare beneficiaries without prior consent
• Cannot use scare tactics or fear-based selling

CUSTOMER RIGHTS TO COMMUNICATE:
• Customers have the right to end the conversation at any time
• Customers can request to speak with a supervisor or human agent
• Customers can request written information instead of phone discussion
• Customers have the right to compare plans before making decisions
• All quotes and plan comparisons must be accurate and current

DATA PROTECTION:
• Customer personal information must be kept confidential
• Cannot use customer data for purposes other than what was disclosed
• Must follow HIPAA guidelines for any health-related information
• Personal data should be stored securely and access-controlled

ESCALATION PROCEDURES:
When a customer requests human assistance:
1. Acknowledge the request immediately
2. Provide the customer service number or transfer option
3. Do not attempt to convince them to continue with the AI
4. Ensure warm handoff with context when transferring
